Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for having taken high-handed and anti-democratic actions in this session and for having proceeded, without a mandate and through the imposition of closure, to abolish the historic Crow Rate, to impose measures relating to taxes on petroleum and natural gas, to cap old age pensions, to create Canagrex, to limit increases in family allowance payments, to change income tax laws, and to increase public debt through additional borrowing and calls upon the Government to seek a mandate by calling a general election without delay.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this Government has put democracy in this country on trial. Canadians are terribly concerned about where this country is going. In a very few years they have seen Canada reduced from a first rate power to one on a par with newly emerging countries. They have seen a nation with an economy in balance, a nation with high employment, reduced to one with a deficit which is so high as to cause concern even in the IMF and cause wonderment about this country's ability to manage its own affairs. They have seen a country that was pulling its weight in NATO and highly regarded for doing so reduced to one which is no longer trusted in the NATO Council.
[DOT]	(mo)
The recent episode in Grenada showed the whole world how the present Government is regarded. Canada was not trusted by the Caribbean nations because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Government of this country have gone out of their way to show softness on Marxism and an affinity for Communist governments which is neither appropriate nor safe in a democratic country like ours.
The Prime Minister went to St. Lucia in the Caribbean last February and stated that Marxist governments would continue to receive Canadian aid. I took him up on this in the House and he repeated the statement. That statement was one of the reasons given by the Prime Minister of St. Lucia as an explanation of why Canada was not consulted about the action taken in Grenada. This Government has admitted it was not consulted about the intervention in Grenada, although its
likelihood was the subject of front page stories in the London Times and Observer, as well as The New York Times in its Sunday edition of October 23. Obviously Government Members do not even read the newspapers. Not only did the Government not know about the intervention, but it apparently was not invited to the consultations which took place following the gruesome murder of Maurice Bishop and several members of his cabinet, along with dozens of innocent civilians the previous Wednesday.
In spite of the fact that Canada has been a major supplier of aid to the Caribbean and that we have a long historical involvement in the area because of its Commonwealth membership, this Government neither took the trouble nor showed any interest in being informed as to what was happening.
We had a famous statement by a junior Minister of State for External Affairs a few days after the grizzly events of October 19 on Grenada when he said that after a "decent interval" Canada would likely recognize the gang which gained power by murdering the incumbents. This was a curious concept of Commonwealth parliamentary government on the part of a chief spokesman for the present Government. Is it any wonder, Sir, that the Government, this one, was not consulted? As a matter of fact, it was not Canada which was not consulted; it was this Government which was not consulted, because of its ideological bias which is only too well known.
We had another example of the same kind of bias in the recent pilgrimage of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) when he visited the Middle East and appeared totally oblivious to what had. been going on there, what was going on there, and what that struggle is all about. Praising the Syrians for their involvement in Lebanon, an involvement based on maintaining a state of instability in the country with guns, tanks and rockets, while there were
7,000	Soviet troops in Syria and the Soviet has poured in billions of dollars in weaponry, was a new height in naivete even for this Government. Or was it naivete? There are a good many Canadians wondering about that question today.
These, Sir, are but a few examples, along with the highest and most persistent unemployment in history and the apparent inability of this Government to distinguish between our friends and allies and our enemies, which have given rise to a growing concern among Canadians as to the direction in which this country is being pushed by the present Government. The spectacle now of the Prime Minister, in a last minute bid for popularity, knocking at the doors of Europe and Asia, portraying himself as some sort of new messiah of world peace, rather than allaying the confusion in our own country, merely serves to increase this concern.

November 15, 1983
Supply
No one can be critical of any sincere and genuine effort toward achieving peace in the world. Such a purpose enjoys universal support. But when, with great fanfare, at a Liberal fund raising dinner, the Prime Minister unveils a master plan for peace, he invites cynicism. No wonder this place, this Parliament, is becoming totally irrelevant in the minds of Canadians. Liberal tactics, Liberal practices, mean announcements not to this House of Commons but announcements to Liberals only, an action described in this morning's written media at best as contemptuous and at worst as downright sleazy.
[DOT] (ms)
It is interesting to note, Sir, that of the five proposals-first, a big five summit conference; second, banning high altitude satellite weapon systems; third, expansion of the non-proliferation treaty; fourth, new initiatives in Geneva; and fifth, restricting non-verifiable IBMs-two of these are aimed directly at the capacity of the United States to mount a deterrent against nuclear attack. On the question of reducing conventional forces in eastern Europe, the Prime Minister has not revealed his solution to the 40,000 Soviet tanks stationed there.
These are hard, practical issues that must be resolved before peace proposals, however attractive on paper, can be taken seriously. While in an abstract way it is commendable for the Prime Minister to pursue solutions in finding peace for the world, there remain serious questions at home, among them the highest unemployment rate in our history for which many Canadians would prefer to see this Government produce some answers. The Government has failed dismally to do so and has instead gone on imposing long-distance solutions with little relation to the problems at hand.
That is another reason for the lack of confidence shown in the polls, a lack of confidence so serious that the only solution at the present time is for the Government to call an election. The Prime Minister of course does not want an election because not only is he worried about the support of the electorate, he cannot even count on the support of his own Party.
Many Liberals across the country are deeply concerned about the manner in which this Government has attempted radically to change the shape and direction of our traditional objectives in this country, our purposes and our institutions, changes in the House of Commons which do not go a yard beyond the knowledge of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader. It is 581 days today that this session of Parliament has been sitting, and there have been 16 closure motions in one session-all records, all destructive of tradition.
There is one tradition though in this country, ever since Confederation, and that is an election once in every four years. But 1 dare say, having regard to the difficulties the Liberals perceive themselves to be in now-de facto are in now-they will cast that tradition aside as well.
By allowing interest rates to rise to unprecedented heights, this Government not only tolerated a record unemployment level, it created it. Because he did not dare lead this country into European style socialism by the front door, the Prime Minister has been doing it by the back door. He has created a bureaucracy in this country which an Auditor General has termed a parallel government, a government within a government. He has created a Frankenstein apparatus employing more people outside the Government than are employed within the Government of Canada. He has created an apparatus responsible directly to himself and his Cabinet with no responsibility to Parliament for day to day operations. He has intervened in every aspect of private and public life as no Government has done in the history of this country.
The National Energy Program puts the petroleum industry in a straitjacket, has creamed off profits and put them in the coffers of the Government. It has destroyed the confidence of investors, confiscated 25 per cent of the frontier lands, driven out over $4 billion in 18 months and cost Canada the Alaska highway natural gas pipeline and the tar sands project because outside investors were afraid to work with this Government. It has now entirely frozen development in my own riding of Yukon. Not content with this it set up CIDC and took over 1,400 service stations at a cost of $2 billion. Canadians are continuing to pay for this although all of the obligations have been met. This is the way this Government has been operating and is why Canadians are nervous and confused. Only an election can clean up the mess and clean out the mess.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext:
We have had evidence of former Liberal Ministers being granted favours. We have had friends of the Prime Minister appointed to high places. We have had mismanagement in Crown corporations and agencies to the point where Canadians are not receiving the services they pay for. We have had a series of unexplainable episodes in Air Canada indicating mismanagement or carelessness in an organization where pleasing the Government has become more important than doing a job. This is why Canadians are uneasy and want an election.
In this House we have had the traditional Crow rate, one of the guarantees of Saskatchewan's entry into Confederation, swept away because of the Government's decision to impose a paper solution on the West. This Government does not care about the West, nor does it care about the East. Its major concern in central Canada appears to be the big contributors to the Liberal Party. They are the ones who have been doing all right under this Government.
To show this Government's contempt for Parliament and the people Parliament represents, it has run this session on for 581 days without a Throne Speech and with no indication of its plans for the future. It introduced two abortive budgets and one it failed to follow through on. It has brought in imposed solutions to the problems it created and those solutions have added to the confusion and uncertainty in the country.
November 15, 1983

In each case its policies have been so obviously self-serving that it has only been able to put them through with closure. It went back on its promises to old age pensioners and retired public servants. It shoved the changes in the Crow rate down the throat of western grain producers. It went back on its undertakings to the Provinces to pay 50 per cent of hospital costs. At the same time it spent money like water to support a hoard of Crown agencies which it itself created and which have not yet been approved by Parliament.
It is significant that when the Government took over Cana-dair four years ago it could have met all of its obligations of $40 million, yet it is now in a deficit position to the tune of over $2 billion. This is directly due to mismanagement by this Government.
The result of this Government's action on the Crow rate is that the western grain producer is now called on to pay for railroad modernization which should have been undertaken years ago out of current revenues. This was not done. The Government will pay enormous subsidies to the railways and extract a proportionate amount from western grain producers in order to compensate for the payments being made to the railways. The Government decided in its usual half baked way to highball through. There is no doubt Canadians will be paying for total confusion in transportation until such time as a Conservative Government can take office and clean up the mess.
Mr. Speaker, the time has come to put an end to this Government and the endless misery that it has caused Canadians. Canadians from coast to coast want an election now. There is an unmistakable message. Canadians have had enough of back door socialism, enough of tinkering, enough of experimentation. They have had enough of lost jobs. They have had enough of bankruptcies. They have had enough of the flight of investment. They have had enough of the stagnation in industry. They want this Government out.
The present Government has reduced Canada to a level nationally and internationally reminiscent of the 1930s. It has done this in order to carry out the Prime Minister's ideological proclivities and to enable its members to keep their own jobs. Having heard the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) trying to explain the Government's position on Grenada two weeks ago and also the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the Middle East, one would have taken them for members of Socialist International.
Canadians have shown in poll after poll that they are fed up. Not all of the Prime Minister's posturing and preening on the international stage, which he loves so well, can change the realities of a situation which has left Canada bereft of policy and leadership. Canadians want a chance to make a choice. They want to put Canada back to work. They want the Trudeau Government out.
They want a new Progressive Conservative Government in its place so that Canada can once again begin to realize its full potential so sadly neglected for too many years. If the NDP

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a great pleasure to have the opportunity to listen to the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). He is one of those individuals who very rarely hides his particular point of view under the sheen or camouflage of what would be considered to be the niceties of parliamentary courtesy.
It is important and useful to have this debate today because we now find out what is at the core of the views of Members opposite. We no longer have the shining images in front of us. We are getting down to the basic goods which are the kind of bar room biases and right-wing rhetoric which they are trying to sell as an alternative to this Government.
We all came to the House this morning with a resolution in front of us dealing with a number of specific issues. What we have heard instead is a great catechism and litany of all the particular prejudices that the Hon. Member for Yukon could drag out from the very depths of his soul. But 1 think it is worth examining some of these presumptions simply to find out if an election would, in fact, solve the problem that the Hon. Member says it would.
Presumably, an election is meant to offer a choice, not simply to criticize the other side. Let us examine what the choices are. The Hon. Member first initiated a major attack on the position on Grenada taken by this Government. His point was that we were not consulted and that we were objecting to the actions taken. Well, the question we must ask is, what was the position of the Conservatives during this period? Where did they stand on the issue? I saw their spokesperson, the Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), on television the other night when he was asked where he stood on this issue. He said: "It is a little bit this way and a little bit that way; we do not stand anywhere on this issue". What kind of choice has been offered regarding that particular problem?
The Hon. Member says that our position was based upon some deep attachment to Marxism. That must be the same motivation for Margaret Thatcher's government whom we also know must have a deep attachment to Marxism if she is to take the same position as this Government. Our position raises very serious questions about invading a sovereign country against the rule of law. Great Britain took the right stand when it raised that issue but Members of the Conservative Party did not have the guts to do that because they do not have the guts to take stands on any issue.
An election should offer a choice. What was the choice that the Conservatives offered us? They did not offer any choice. They said: "We are not sure we like what you are doing but we do not have anything to offer in return." That is the real question. But what are the alternatives?

November 15, 1983
Supply
The Hon. Member for Yukon goes on to say that our position in NATO is totally without credibility. If that is the case then 1 would ask Members of the House why it was, when the Prime Minister undertook his mission of the past week, that the major leaders of those countries not only invited him but welcomed him for that kind of discussion.
NATO itself is an organization not dedicated to war mong-ering or to sabre rattling, as the Hon. Member for Yukon would like to believe to be the case; it is an organization dedicated to maintaining peace in this world. Those countries recognize there has to be collective security but at the same time they recognize that initiatives have to be taken for arms control and disarmament. Again, I ask the question, where is the Conservative Party on the issue of arms control and disarmament? Where is that Party's proposals, ideas and initiatives?
What do we hear from them as to what kind of solutions the Conservatives would bring to perhaps the most serious, significant issue that faces mankind? Have we heard the new Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) give us his plan for peace? Have we heard what kind of proposals he would raise to reduce world tensions and reduce the enormous agglomeration of arms buildup? Not a word have we heard, Mr. Speaker. Not a peep. Not a single sentence has been uttered in terms of the proposals which the Progressive Conservative Party would offer Canadians in searching out ways of dealing with the matter that affects every Canadian deep inside of how we reduce world tension. At least we are trying to do the right thing. We are not hiding behind a barrage of right-wing rhetoric; we are trying to take initiatives that will help people secure some feeling that somebody is doing something. We are not simply allowing a willy-nilly escalation of the arms race; we are trying to use the position of credibility and confidence which this Prime Minister has built up over the last decade and we are trying to develop that position around the world. W'e are being received and accepted in doing so.
Surely if the question were asked by Canadians as to who has the kind of right and reason to pursue arms control, either the Hon. Member for Yukon or the Prime Minister, we know what the answer would be. At least people recognize that the Prime Minister has won that confidence by his initiatives overseas, not by the kinds of fits of silliness that we have seen displayed by the Hon. Member for the Yukon this morning.
We have also heard about the failure of this Government to deal with unemployment. We recognize and have recognized over the past several years what a serious and tragic consequence that has been. We have also recognized that it is a problem that has faced every single country in the world. We have not been immune to the economic recession that has taken place worldwide. The real issue is that we try to do something about it.
All the Hon. Member for Yukon would have to do is to open his ears from time to time during Question Period and listen to the kinds of initiatives that have been taken by this Government. In the last budget we had $2.4 billion in new capital
recovery projects which affect every region of this country regardless of who represents the region. The Hon. Member might be prepared to listen to the initiatives taken under direct employment. It was the government of which he was a Member that abolished direct employment programs. What would have happened to this country if the program of the so-called Conservative Party which abolished direct employment programs had been allowed to be maintained during that period of recession? Who would have helped the hundreds of thousands of people who were given work, support and useful activity through the Canada Works programs, the community development programs and the work sharing programs? What about the billions of dollars that were spent to give people that kind of support when they were out of work?
This group across from us would not have helped. They say they do not believe in that. They are the great free enterprisers. They were going to let the market take care of the problem. We saw how the market took care of it. It simply abandoned those people. This Government is not prepared to abandon those who are unemployed. We did not abolish direct employment programs; we brought them back into place. Thank God we did so that the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who were faced with unemployment in that market system were given.some support by this Government.
The Hon. Member for Yukon mentioned this "terrible travesty" of the National Energy Program. We saw the statements by his leader of this last week that he would get rid of it. He would abolish it. Does that mean he would go back to world prices, that he would ask Canadians to pay the full world price?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

Is that what the Conservative Party is going to offer people in an election, that they will pay even higher energy prices? Is that what the Leader of the Opposition was stating last week in Calgary? We are not too sure because the Leader of the Opposition said one thing in Calgary but seemed to change his mind when he got to Edmonton. By the time he got to Edmonton he said: "No, I am not going to abolish it". Then one of his backbenchers here in Ottawa had a different story, which simply means the Conservatives are like a vaudeville team. You hit a new town, you play a new act. It has a different tune and a different song, depending upon the crowd you are playing to.
We would have liked to hear from the Hon. Member for Yukon this morning, in his diatribe against this Party and this Government's energy policy, what his Party stands for. What is his energy policy? Is it to get rid of the National Energy Program and have world prices?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: It is to get rid of you.

speechtext: Is that what his Party is standing for? If that is the case, Mr. Speaker, why do the Conservatives not say so? Why do they not have the guts to get up and say so?

speechtext: Why does the Leader of the Opposition keep changing his tune every time he hits a different town and why does he not stand up and say what he believes in?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: I thought this resolution couched in the words of the Hon. Member for Yukon is meant to say that we have forgotten Parliament. Has the Leader of the Opposition forgotten Parliament that he has to go to Calgary and Edmonton to give his particular panegyric on the energy program? Is he afraid to come into the House of Commons and tell us where he stands? Is that the problem with him? Is it that the Conservatives do not want to use Parliament as their forum for discussion and ideas? Here is the Hon. Member for Yukon saying that the Prime Minister has avoided Parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: Now we are finding out that the Leader of the Opposition also avoids Parliament. The Conservatives cannot have it both ways. 1 suppose it is only natural that leaders of parties are going to go across the country and make policy statements. I am not being critical of the Leader of the Opposition; goodness knows, I would not want to. 1 know how sensitive he is to criticism and how closely he takes it to heart. I would not want to comment on that. Of course, the Leader of the Opposition has the right to make statements in Calgary and change his mind in Edmonton. The fact of the matter is he is showing the same disregard for Parliament, if we use the logic of the Hon. Member for Yukon, as he is castigating the Prime Minister for so doing. What is this debate all about?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: It is the Government that is accountable.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: What is this kind of criticism being levelled at? Is it that political leaders are not supposed to go across the country and talk to groups of people and make their own statements?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: Governments are accountable.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: If that is the case, we would like to see the Leader of the Opposition in Parliament more often telling us where his "Government" stands.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES

Let us go on to some other issues. The Member for Yukon has raised the spectre of the Crow. He said this Government has brought in this piece of legislation without any consultation in the West, that it is going to

destroy western Canada with total disregard for Parliament. That is pretty interesting, Mr. Speaker. It was three years ago that two major farm organizations, the Prairie Farm Commodity Coalition and the Western Agricultural Conference, asked that the Crow be changed and said that the real issue in western Canada was the failure to provide for a proper capacity to move grain to market. The kind of threat that we were looking at was the inability of this country's export market to be able to ensure its customers delivery on time at a decent price, and a government must take action to make that come about.
We could have followed the advice of the Conservative Party, which was to take no action at all, to freeze the program. This would have meant that by 1985-1986 we would have had a railway system that could not carry those goods to market. We would not have been able to sell those goods to the customers we have. We had a policy from the Conservative Party of "do nothing", of freeze. That was the word the Conservatives used. Do you know what a freeze is, Mr. Speaker? It is being frozen in position, afraid to make a decision.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: Like Munro has done to the Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext:
That is what we had from Hon. Members of the Conservative Party. They were scared of making a decision because they knew there was no unanimity in their ranks as to what the position should be. Their only recourse was to oppose and be obstructive. That was their only recourse. It was not that they had a position; it was not what they were prepared to do to deal with the looming crisis in the railway system. They were going to say; "Let us continue a few ad hoc items; we will buy some more hopper cars here and give a few more subsidies there". What they were afraid of doing was attacking the fundamental, central problem, which is that every bushel of grain that was moved was losing money for the mover of that grain.
That group which says it believes in the market economy should at least have a minimal understanding of economics. One does not invest money in something one loses money at doing; if one makes an investment, one at least has to receive a proper return.

The Hon. Member indicated that the Government could not bring in a Throne Speech. even allowed to debate the Bill because we were engaged in the gymnastics of parliamentary obstruction, the major product of the particular evil genius of the Hon. Member opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

speechtext:
Of course there is a certain cant in all he says. We heard the Hon. Member for Yukon say today that Parliament was being abused, that we were using closure when we should not. All we were doing was what a responsible government should do-make decisions, run the affairs of the country and attempt to overcome the obstructions of Hon. Members opposite.
I would like to quote the words of a self-acknowledged parliamentary expert who, in writing to another self-acknowledged parliamentary expert, said: "Having said that, our understanding of a parliamentary democracy does not allow us to agree with you that a majority government, however bad, does not have the right to govern in accordance with established tradition and precedents". Guess who that parliamentary expert was?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext: "Established tradition and precedents"; that is the key.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT MEASURES
speechtext:
I will give the House one guess. Who was it? It was the Hon. Member for Yukon who indicated that the Government had the right to decide and should not be obstructed by the minority. That is the question. If we allowed the House to be so convoluted and overturned by the sort of parliamentary terrorism we faced in the Chamber day after day, we could not continue with the business of the nation and the affairs of the House.
1 cite, for the basis of my argument, the very words of the Hon. Member for Yukon when he indicated that the Government must decide. That is what we were doing. We were trying to make a decision in the House which would not only bring about a major expansion of the railways but also address the very issue the Hon. Member said we were not addressing- the question of unemployment. We recognize full well that the way to get the engine of the economy going is by providing some stimulus, some investment and some incentive for the private market to begin to work.
We have not heard lately from the Leader of the Opposition on the subject, but when he first came here he said that his objective was jobs, jobs, jobs. of the new Leader of the Opposition. We were putting people in his riding back to work with our legislation. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first of all to make it clear to the House that we substantially agree with the criticisms contained in the motion put forward by the Hon. House Leader for the Official Opposition and we will, of course, support the main thrust of the motion. 1 say that so that there will be no doubt in the mind of any Hon. Member about where we stand.
1 would like, however, to say that I must confess to having some difficulty in taking the criticism of the Conservative Party seriously. I have looked back over the course of the last two years. I am firmly convinced that the Government has failed to act reasonably in almost every single area of concern to the majority of Canadians and I am prepared to level criticism at the Government for the hamhanded way in which it has dealt with the economy, its neglect of people who are unemployed, its inability or unwillingness to come to grips with high interest rates and its general attitude toward the concerns of the Provinces.
However, I find it very difficult to accept at face value the criticisms being levelled by Hon. Members of the Conservative Party. They have come forward on every side of every issue raised in the House since 1980. They have attempted to be all things to all people on every single area of policy since the House was called into session after the election in the winter of 1980.
It is hard to accept that Members of the Conservative Party are serious about doing anything to try to improve the disaster that has been created as a result of Liberal mismanagement. If you sit as an observer and watch the Tories in action, you cannot help but wonder just what they stand for. They have a spokesman not only for every issue, but a spokesman for each side of every issue. If, for example, you want to see high energy prices, if you are part of the lobby group that is looking for high energy prices, you go to the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). He will gladly speak for you. However, if you are a consumer concerned about high energy prices, eager to keep the price down so that you can pay for it with your meagre wages, speak to the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott). He will gladly get up and speak on your behalf.
If you are in favour of testing the Cruise missile in Canada, the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) is your man. He will get up at any time and explain how we must have this
November 15, 1983

continued escalation of nuclear warfare weapons. If, however, you are one of the groups in one part of Canada or another that is opposed to the testing of the Cruise and you do not want to see it go ahead, just get yourself on the mailing list of the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean). He will be glad to speak for you.
If you think there is some need to cut Government expenditures, contact the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), the slasher. He will be happy to tell you of all the wonderful cutting that the Tory Party is going to do. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) will be glad to rise and speak on your behalf with passion.

However, if on the other hand if you think jacked up diplomacy is the way, march on and trample them underfoot, cut off all dialogue and isolate ourselves from the rest of the world, again there is the Member for York-Peel. He is your man. He will be glad to speak for you.
I could go on. I suspect I could take a whole day and go through the Conservative caucus one by one. You would find on every single issue, no matter what position you take, no matter what side of the issue you are for, no matter how adamantly you are opposed, a Conservative happily standing up to speak for you.
Some people may say that is democracy, that that is the democracy of the Conservative Party, that it shows they really do understand the nation. However, what would be their policy if in office? When you come right down to it, who would win the tug of war? Which of the various Members speaking for the Conservative Party actually enunciates the policy they would pursue? That is the key question that must surely be in the minds of the majority of Canadians.
Canadians are sick up to the back of their throats with this Liberal Government, and quite rightly so. Canadians have seen this Liberal Government for what it is; hard hearted, incompetent, incapable, posturing at all times. However, sick as they are with that bunch, how could any clear minded individual possibly go out and support this rag-tag bunch from the Conservative Party? How could anyone do that?
1 have said this before, I think it is true, it was true when I said it the first time and I would not say it again if it were not still true: the Conservative Party have more positions than Masters and Johnson. They do not know what they stand for. All they stand for is getting into government. All they stand for is getting rid of the Grits. I want to get rid of the Grits as well, but I want to put in place a policy that makes sense for Canada. I want to give Canadians a clear and unequivocal choice. I want to afford Canadians the opportunity to vote for something and not simply against something. That is the choice that Canadians will ultimately be forced to make. Are they going to vote simply against a very bad Government as exemplified by the Liberal Government of the last two years? Will they vote against it by voting for a pig in the poke, some kind of take a chance and let us hope that things work out all right?
The Conservatives will not tell us what they are going to do. They ask Canadians to give them a chance and maybe they will be surprised. My God, maybe they will be surprised. 1 do not believe it is unreasonable to think that the Tory attitude is not at all unlike the attitude of their Conservative friend in British Columbia, Bill Bennett. If the Conservatives were ever to form a Government, and heaven forbid it should ever happen, I would expect to see them follow the exact same line of that heartfelt Premier of British Columbia, that man of compassion who does not respect order, tradition and people's rights, who tramples all over them at every turn and does not give a damn about the impact of his policies. That is their Conservative friend in British Columbia. That is what the

public of Canada will risk getting if it elects a Conservative government.
There are positive things which should be done in this country. What we must do for starters is come to grips with the interest rates being charged by the financial institutions. We must bring that interest rate spread down to a level which will ensure that the people of Canada will be able to purchase the goods they need for themselves and their families. We must bring that interest rate spread down to a point at which small businesses will be able to continue to provide the services which they have historically provided. We must decide now that that is a priority. But neither the Liberals nor the Conservative are prepared to take that measure.
We must begin now to build homes in this country to meet the needs of the people at prices they can afford to pay and, in the process, put people back to work. We must begin now to establish a new transportation policy in order that we not only can build for the future, but can assure that the port facilities inland and on the coast are modernized and capable of meeting the requirements of the next generation. We must start now to make sure that the agricultural implements industry in Canada is refurbished and regenerated so that the farmers of Canada will be able to stay in the forefront of competition.
Let me say now, Mr. Speaker, in order that I do not miss the opportunity, that I intend to move the following amendment just to show the kind of positive things one should expect to see from a new government in office. I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell):
That the motion be amended by deleting the period after the word "delay"and substituting the following therefor:
"in order that a new government receive a mandate to implement the following program for job creation and economic development; the establishment of lower interest rates and the restoration of traditional interest rate spreads between loans and savings, the introduction of a major housing construction program, the implementation of the Auto Task Force Report, the revitalization of the farm implements manufacturing sector, the upgrading of all vital transportation systems including inland and coastal ports and a new commitment to reforestation and forestry sector development; and the full restoration of public sector and collective bargaining rights.
That is the kind of thing which the Canadian public have a right to expect to hear from those who vie for office, from those who want to govern the country.
There are other things which must be contained in a program for the revitalization of Canada. There are other direct policies which must be supported, not by one or two Hon. Members but by all Hon. Members of whatever party forms the government. We must develop a mining equipment manufacturing industry in this country because it makes no sense that we should be so rich in resources and so poor in the manufacturing of mining equipment. We must utilize in our own interests western Canadian coal and the creation of electrical power in Provinces which are now purchasing it from outside the country. We must develop in Canada a forestry machinery industry because, again, it makes no sense for a country so rich in forestry resources not to have available the most technologically advanced forest machinery industry.
We must complete the East-West pipeline in order that Canadians can be self-sufficient in energy and we can create in Canada a self-sufficiency which will allow us to develop industrially over the course of the next 10, 15 or 20 years. We must work at developing an import substitution policy for Canada so that Canadian manufacturers large and small can be given a direction in which to look to replace those manufactured products which have been brought into this country from offshore which we ourselves could be manufacturing.
There are in this country people who are dedicated to putting those kinds of policies in place. There are people who would like to see full employment in Canada, who would like to see the youth of this land given an opportunity to go to work rather than leaving school only to find there is no work for them in any part of the land.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the public of Canada are not going to receive those kinds of policies from either the Liberals-no matter what they do in terms of their leadership-or from the Conservatives, because the Conservatives are not dedicated as a team to developing a single set of policies which would make sense for the future of the country. The time will come, Mr. Speaker, when the Conservatives will be asked to stand up and be counted on these issues. There will be a time when the public will say to the Conservative Party: "You cannot be on every side. You cannot speak with a forked tongue forever. You simply must say what it is you truly want to see happen."
1 suggest that the only Party in Canada which is prepared to make those kinds of categorical statements, and to back them up with action, is the New Democratic Party. I would welcome an election. I would welcome the opportunity to take on this bunch of two-faced, double-talking individuals who refuse to offer constructive opposition and intelligent alternatives to this washed-out Liberal bunch.

Member talks about hopper cars, but when were many of those hopper cars brought in? When the Hon. Member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Mazankowski) was the Minister of Transport the very large increase in hopper cars took place. This was not accomplished by changing the Crow but by sitting down with the railways and the prairie Governments. As a representative of the federal Government he asked them how to solve this capacity problem. Great steps were taken in that respect.
I want to deal with some other issues raised in this motion. Another reason people in this country feel a change is needed is the economic mismanagement of the Government. Today, as a result of the Government's economic mismanagement, roughly 25 cents of every tax dollar collected now goes to service the debt. I found the remarks of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre rather interesting and 1 agreed with his views in the way he formed his question. However, the fact remains that the Government has a very serious debt problem. It is not only very serious because of its size and the drain it is causing on the general accounts of Canada, but in my view it is jeopardizing the very social programs which Canadians want to keep in place. That is very serious.
We can be very partisan in the House-and I have been- but I want to say to the Government that we look forward to seeing the Canada Health Act. We want to know what programs the Government will propose. In light of the economic reality we face in Canada, we want to know how the programs which are now in place-which we want to preserve and strengthen but also take cognizance of the realities that we as Canadians must face in terms of the demography of the country-will be able to meet those two objectives in view of the economic mismanagement that we have seen during the last 15 years and which is now seriously jeopardizing many of those safety nets.
While we can talk about many issues which have a public profile, such as user fees, extra billing and opting out, the real issue we must face is the ability to maintain and enhance programs in light of this Government's economic mismanagement over the last 15 years. That is the point. I welcome the proposals from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) for meeting those two realities.
If Canadian business people or Canadians generally were paying 25 cents out of every dollar just to pay interest on a debt, I know what their bankers would be doing. Their bankers would be calling them in and would want to look at their financial statements. That is what Canadians must be worried about today with respect to the Government.
I want to say to the Government in all seriousness that the greatest negative legacy it is leaving behind is that its economic mismanagement is jeopardizing that which Canadians believe to be right and properly part of their collective protection or safety net in our society. The Government cannot dispute that because those are hard facts. A report on pensions is to be tabled approximately in the middle of December. Pensions are a very serious issue without doubt and we have
had a task force on pensions and have had a green paper. In my experience and I am sure in the experience of every Member of the House, one of the most critical problems in this respect concerns widows, especially those between the ages of 55 and 65 who do not have a safety net to fall back on. How do we address this question of pensions while keeping in mind again the economic reality that we face as Canadians as a result of the economic mismanagement of the Government?
We can also talk about the maintenance of health care. The Minister has said that the federal Government has not withdrawn its share of funding in any way. However, when we look at the demography of Canada and the demands in that system, the Provinces which have primary responsibility in that area recognize the need for alternate care, preventive health care, home care and community based care. Where are the Minister's plans? How will we address those questions in view of the economic mismanagement of the Government? Those are the legacies being left behind.
While we can be partisan in the House, and I can possibly be as partisan as anyone in this place, the point is that the Government's legacy is that it has spent money on things for which Canadians today and in the future are being asked to pay when the very fundamental and essential issues which have not been dealt with are now in jeopardy. That is the Government's legacy.
Therefore, this motion calls upon the Government to do the honourable thing and that is to call an election. It is the respectable thing to do. The polls have indicated that many Canadians are absolutely convinced that there is a need for a change in Government. Some have said that my leader and this Party will form the next Government of Canada. I believe that to be the case. But we are not only a Government in waiting, Canada is waiting. The country is waiting for a change. The country is waiting to have confidence returned and to bring optimism back to it. It is not only the Progressive Conservative Party but Canada that is waiting. The NDP do not want a Conservative Government in Canada to the extent that they will do whatever is in their power to return the Liberals and form a coalition and make deals with them.
I will leave this point with you, Mr. Speaker, and with Canadians. I say that Canada and Canadians are waiting. When Canadians want a change of Government, when democracy demands a change in Government and the democratic system must be cleansed, Canadians cannot afford the luxury of voting for a third party, because the experience in Canada for having a third party has always been the return of the Liberals. Therefore, I say that Canadians are waiting for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) to take his rightful place as the Prime Minister of Canada and to bring back to Canada the hope and the potential that should be ours as Canadians.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EDUCATIONAL SERVICES FOR INMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past ten years a few Canadian universities have developed a successful, cost-effective, rehabilitation program in several penitentiaries. The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) has already killed this program in Quebec, Ontario, and the Prairies. He is about to transform the one in British Columbia into something quite different from the successful program it has been. Meanwhile, Canadians are being misled into believing that the university programs will be continued. In fact the educational tinkering of the Solicitor General will result in their disappearance. The Canadian Association for Adult Education recently sent an analysis of the matter to Canadian university presidents.
Also, the Solicitor General proposes to make students pay part of the cost despite the fact a study has found that this will put an end to the programs and to the human and social benefits involved. The Solicitor General has been advised by virtually the entire educational community that he is making a serious mistake. He completely ignores the advice. Why, especially in the field of education in which the federal Government is not particularly competent?
Enlightened Canadians believe that one of the primary purposes of penitentiaries is education or re-education. In view of the arrogance and stubbornness of the Solicitor General regarding this mandated responsibility, I suggest he consult with the Department of the Secretary of State, or with experienced provincial educational officials, with the aim of modernizing his dated approach toward penitentiaries and rehabilitation.

CHOICE OF LIBERAL PARTY FUNCTION FOR SPEECH ON PEACE INITIATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed. I must admit that I was looking forward to hearing the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tell the House about his pilgrimage to Europe to discuss his peace initiatives. Unfortunately, these days, any important speeches made by the Prime Minister seem to occur at Liberal functions. Much as I like to hear good rhetoric, I would really feel most uncomfortable attending a function designed for the good Grits of our country. Therefore my absence is understandable, as would be that of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) who has already stated his abhorrence at receiving invitations to Liberal functions.
My point today is that the Prime Minister should not have chosen a Liberal fund-raising event to disclose details of his efforts to help the cause of peace in the world. Until yesterday, when I heard the news that once again Members of Parliament were the last people to hear important information, I respected him for his efforts. Now it appears quite evident that the Prime Minister is taking the opportunity to add another feather to his cap among his Liberal cohorts. This is definitely not the proper way to go about such matters.
I agree with a daily publication when it indicated that the Liberal movers and shakers got feeling a little cocky and light-headed about all the good press received from the Prime Minister's peace initiatives, that they had to gloat, and that they had to use it to make their troops feel good. The fact that

November 15, 1983
the Prime Minister failed to make a statement to the House and chose instead to speak to a Grit fund-raising bunfest leaves only one conclusion, that the whole exercise was designed to enhance his shrunken political stature.

REASONS FOR OPPOSITION BY NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal use of closure to impose Bill C-155 on an unwilling and deeply resentful western Canada underlines how far the Government has strayed from the democratic principles of consent and accountability. We in the New Democratic Party make no apologies for all-out opposition to a Bill that is unwanted, unfair, and undemocratic. We point with pride to a saving of more than $15 million for western Canadian farmers by delaying the freight rate increases which would have been imposed on August 1. We condemn the Government for advising the railways to break the law by ignoring the 60-day filing period for rate increases and imposing higher rates on January 1, 1984.
The Government's action on Bill C-155 was wholly typical. No mandate was sought by the Government to change the Crow rate in the 1980 election. Representations made by electors and elected representatives in the House of Commons were ignored. These representations included 30,000 signatures on petitions filed by the New Democratic Party, and another 7,000 signatures from organizations and individuals who favoured the New Democratic plan to keep the Crow rate and upgrade the railway system.
The then Minister of Transport admitted on May 16 that he had received more than 38,000 signatures favouring Crow retention, and only 69 favouring Crow change. This Act is a testimonial to a Government that puts people last.

subtopic: USE OF POPPY SYMBOL BY PEACE ACTIVISTS
USE OF POPPY SYMBOL BY PEACE ACTIVISTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise while Hon. Members' memories are still warm after the many ceremonies held this past weekend at cenotaphs across Canada to honour veterans of two world wars and the Korean war. Radical elements of the anti-Cruise missile protest movement had the shabby disrespect to drag the Royal Canadian Legion's symbol of remembrance, the poppy, through the political mud on November 11.
I am sure most thoughtful Canadians who quietly protest Cruise testing in the country would agree with me that Remembrance Day is not now, and never will be, political; the poppy is not political. But these diabolically political and professional protesters simply do not recognize the difference between their peace symbols and the poppy:
In Flanders Fields the poppies blow between the crosses, row on row ....
We are the dead.
John McCrae's poem signifies to me, that the poppy is a symbol of remembrance for the fallen. It is definitely not meant as a "peacenik's" peace symbol.
The poem continues:
Take up our quarrel with the foe . . .
To me, Mr. Speaker, that does not mean quarrelling among ourselves in a free Canada. What these unruly protesters fail to remember is that had so many valiant men and women not fought and died for freedom, these peaceniks would not have the democratic freedom to protest against anything at any time.
To hundreds of thousands of veterans across the country the red poppy is the symbol of the blood that was shed in the name of freedom. The poppy must remain the sacred symbol of remembrance of the dead in Flanders fields.
November 15, 1983

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: POLAND-PLEA FOR GRANTING OF EXIT VISAS TO FAMILIES OF LANDED IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time there are hundreds of families separated due to the recent crisis in Poland. Individuals who have been granted permanent residence in Canada anxiously await reunification with their family members who are still in Poland. Many of these families have been separated for two to three years and, as a result, are undergoing mental anguish, particularly in the case of the children who are deprived of proper family security.
Many of these individuals have exhausted all legal avenues open to them to bring their families to Canada. Today, ten such individuals are in their ninth day of a hunger strike in front of the Polish consulate in Toronto, and close to 1,000 petitioners have already indicated their support for this protest.
Family members in Poland have met all Canadian immigration requirements. However, they are being continuously refused the appropriate exit documents by Polish officials, which would allow them to be reunited with their families in Canada. Each family has encountered an average of four to six refusals of these exit documents from Polish authorities.
I appeal to the Canadian Government on grounds of human compassion to continue to make successful representations to the Polish Government on behalf of all of these families and other families when the husbands, wives and children want to live together and not be separated.

about what I have been doing. He can read my speeches and my statement. However, in so far as tabling letters, or making letters public between myself and other leaders of Government is concerned, that not only is not customary, Mr. Speaker, but it would be breaking every diplomatic rule.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition refers to a clear cut undertaking

between himself and myself when we had that conversation. I repeat, there is a clear cut undertaking that one does not make public exchanges of letters between heads of Government. If the President of the United States wants to make his exchange public, and we can find out from the ambassador if he wants to make it public, that is fine. However, I do not intend making my letters public, the ones that I sent to the various heads of Government, because there is a clear cut understanding that that is not the way we are operating. Even when 1 met the leaders last week, we undertook not to go out and make a detailed report of what we had done. We are waiting for other members of the alliance, the other powers involved, to see what we are talking about. Perhaps later, if there are some possible results, we will make them public, but certainly not now.
Once again, if the Leader of the Opposition thinks he has an undertaking from the American President to make his letter public, that is his affair of course. I do not see how he could possibly have that undertaking, but he says he seems to have it from someone.
As far as discussing the subject and making a report in the House of Commons are concerned, today is an opposition day. If it is so important I do not know why the Leader of the Opposition has not made a speech himself, why he has not made the subject of international relations and peace-seeking the subject of the opposition day. The Leader of the Opposition smiles. His Members are smiling as well. It would be interesting to know what they think about international relations. They have not chosen the subject. It is their day.
I repeat, I am happy to answer questions. As a matter of fact I was surprised that the Opposition Party did not ask any questions in the week that I was here after I made my Guelph speech. A lot of people commented on it. The Leader of the Opposition commented on it outside the House, but it did not seem worthy of the attention of the Opposition. I did not know they would suddenly be interested, but suddenly they are. Good. Let us have a debate on it.

CYPRUS-DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE BY TURKISH CYPRIOTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister who, at his August 30 press conference in Athens, Greece, commented on the situation in Cyprus. As the Prime Minister is udoubtedly aware, there has been a declaration of independence on the part of certain Turkish Cypriots on that island proclaiming a new country with respect to the northern part of Cyprus. What is the official response of the Government of Canada to this declaration of independence, and when in fact was the first time that he learned that such a declaration was going to be made?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CYPRUS-DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE BY TURKISH CYPRIOTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the official position of the Government of Canada is that it recognizes the Government in Cyprus which already exists, and with which we have good relations. It is a member of the Commonwealth, and we continue to want to have good relations with that Government. Insofar as the declaration of independence of a part of that country is concerned, we regret it. The Hon. Member asks when we first heard of it. I first heard of it this morning. Perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs can elaborate as to the exact moment we were informed of it.
The Hon. Member, being the official critic for External Relations, would know that the possibility or the threat of a declaration of independence by the Turkish part of Cyprus has been mooted for quite a while, certainly for some months. That is why we very strongly encouraged the initiative of the Secretary General of the United Nations toward a compromise between the communities in Cyprus which are in conflict. It is not something that had been unheard of. We regret that the compromise proposals put forward by the Secretary General were not given a chance to succeed before this event happened.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. MCGRATH-QUESTION ON UNEMPLOYMENT ANSWERED BY MRS. EROLA-RULING OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext:
Yesterday, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) raised a point of order following the daily Question Period regarding a question asked by the Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall). The question was addressed to the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) but was answered by the Hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola).
Our practice is very clear in this matter and I would like to quote Citation 361 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition:
A question may not be asked of a Minister in another capacity, such as being responsible for a Province, or part of a Province, or as spokesman for a racial or religious group.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker Lamoureux puts the matter very succinctly in a ruling given on October 16, 1968, and I quote:
-a Minister may be asked questions relating to a department for which he has ministerial responsibility or acting ministerial responsibility, but a Minister cannot be asked, nor can he answer questions in another capacity, such as being responsible for a province, or a part of a province-
I am concerned, however, that the question posed by the Hon. Member for Timiskaming referred to actions of another Minister, while it was directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. That complicates the matter from the point of view of the Chair. It is difficult for the Chair to make a ruling to the effect that any Minister named in a question should not have some right to respond to the allegations in a question.
However, the general rule that Ministers should be asked questions and should answer questions relating to their primary ministerial responsibility is a basic rule of the procedure of the House.

What is the mandate of the Provincial Analysis and Liaison Secretariat of the Federal-Provincial Relations Office?

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The mandate of the Liaison and Integration Secretariat (formerly the Provincial Analysis and Liaison Secretariat) is to ensure effective flows of information and data on provincial and regional concerns, views and initiatives in order to provide timely and accurate assessments of the current status of federal-provincial relations at the national, regional and provincial levels and to identify any emerging issues affecting federal-provincial relations in each of the Provinces.
The Secretariat also co-ordinates the preparation of briefing material for major undertakings (for example, First Ministers' Conferences and bilateral meetings between the Prime Minister and Premiers), and for the provision of advice on specific federal-provincial issues of major importance.
Further, as part of the liaison and integration function, the Secretariat also has responsibility for managing the Prime Minister's correspondence with each of the Premiers.

Of course, there was a big decline in gas wells for the very valid reason that the market in the United States is such that the Americans cannot take any more gas. speechtext:
The motion says that this House wants to have an election. This morning the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) indicated that in his view the motion calling for an election was "frivolous, irrelevant and makes no sense". 1 want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, and Hon. Members of this House, that so far as I understand the people of this country, and certainly the people in my own riding, the Minister of Transport is dead wrong when he thinks the people of this country do not want an election. People in this country desperately want an election, Mr. Speaker. I believe, indeed, that if every Hon. Member of this House thought about this for a second and remembered the last time he was in his own constituency, particularly during the week of recess, and he took the same opportunity that many of us did, he would know exactly how his constituents feel. People in the constituency of Rosedale, people in the constituencies of Toronto where 1 spent that week, want a change. They want a change badly. If you listen to those people in the constituencies they will tell you things you need to hear about whether or not we need an election. I listened to the people in my own constituency all week long. 1 believe that every Hon. Member would have had the same experience as myself in listening to what they had to say. They have concern, Mr. Speaker. Their number one concern is jobs and financial security. That is the first concern of the people 1 talked to.
There is, Mr. Speaker, 11.1 per cent unemployed in this country. There are 1,346,000 people counted who are unemployed. If you add those who live in areas of the country where there is no opportunity for work at all, the figure is well over 1.5 million people without work. People need to have a job in order to look after their responsibilities. It is something which goes to the very core of the lives of people. What they have had for four years as of February, in the face of that awesome
unemployment, is words, words, words; numbers, numbers, numbers, and programs no end. With all the words, all the numbers and all the programs, the reason that the people do not believe the Government, Mr. Speaker, is that they know a hard fact, which is that beneath all those programs and pronouncements by Ministers, there is the underlying reality of chronic unemployment in this country which will not go away, and which is scaring hell out of people.
When you ask the people, Mr. Speaker, they will tell you that their first concern is jobs and financial security. Twenty-four point four per cent of the people under the age of 25 and who have finished their education are without a job. Is that not a great way to start out in this country, knowing that no matter how hard you try or how much education you have, 25 per cent of you are going to be unemployed?

The first concern that people have is jobs and financial security. That is the first reason they want an election.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, people talk about taxes. My constituents talk to me about taxes and I know they talk to Hon. Members about taxes.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member says "Rosedale". If he knew more about the city he came from, which is supposed to be Toronto, he would understand that in my riding we have people who have been waiting for years for this Government to produce what is promised. What bothers them most about taxes is not only that they are too high. No matter what level of Government you are in, taxes are always too high. Whether they are working people, small business people, artists and writers, they know the system is no longer fair and equitable. It is unjust, unfair and unworkable. That is why when they look at taxes they say to themselves, how is it that a system could go so wrong in such a short space of time? This is an important matter, Mr. Speaker, because in our system of Government taxes are voluntary. The only way people will voluntarily pay their taxes is if they feel the system is fair and just. But they do not see that. What they see is a Department of National Revenue which is just about out of control.
November 15, 1983

Two weeks ago we had a motion from the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), to which this House agreed unanimously, to examine the unjust and unworkable rules applying to artists and writers in this country in the face of the reinterpretation of the law by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres). Despite that, the Minister and his Department continue to apply those rules. He made the interpretation, he can change it, but he does not. That is one example of why people in this country are increasingly trying to avoid taxes in ways which they would not have contemplated in the past. As they do that, the Department becomes more oppressive and makes the assumption that people are guilty until proven innocent. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that when you talk to people in my constituency, indeed in every constituency, there is going to be a day of reckoning for this Government when it tries to explain how it let loose the Department of National Revenue and the way it has been going for the last couple of years.
The third thing my constituents talk about is peace, Mr. Speaker. Peace is not a Party matter. There is no one, whether it is from the NDP, the Liberal or the Conservative Parties, who has a monopoly on or concern for peace. It is an issue which transcends this House and our politics. Everyone I have talked to feels the same way no matter what his role in life. They are more frightened these days because they read in the paper, hear on the radio and watch on television a kind of slow escalation. That is why, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced he was going on a mission to see what he could do with respect to world peace, I know how my constituents felt. They wished him well. Better than that, some of them prayed for him because they need peace and want it so badly. That is why it was even more incumbent than normal on the Prime Minister to bring what he found out to the House and allow the House, and therefore all the people of this country, to deal with the matter as best we can at this time. Peace is not a question of Party, it is not a monopoly of any Party. In a way, not bringing it to this House diminished the Prime Minister's mission. He still has an opportunity and I hope he takes it.
Fourth, Mr. Speaker, my constituents talk about the Government and Parliament. I do not think it will come as a surprise to any Member here that they are very skeptical. They do not trust the Government to understand their problems, and they are skeptical of this House's ability to solve those problems. The more the Government and this House become removed from the people, the more people do not pay any attention to it and the more the national community begins to divide. That is why far more people than I would have thought-and I ask Hon. Members to think about their own constituencies-paid attention to the issue of parliamentary reform. They know that this is the one national free institution which will allow us to deal with our problems. They know it still ought to be what John Stuart Mill once called it, the nation's committee of grievances and its committee of concerns. That is why they supported parliamentary reform, and that is why it was supported by all Party representatives
Supply
on the committee concerned. That is why they are also concerned about why the work of that committee has not proceeded. They know it is only this institution which can help.
Not only do they have concerns about jobs, taxes, peace and the future of our institutions, but they also know what they want. That is not always the same thing and it is not always explained in the same way, but what they want is something very vague and not something small. If I can put it in a few words, Mr. Speaker, they want to start again. They want a rebirth, a renaissance, a revitalization of this country. Nothing less. That is what they are looking for today. They want world class investments, world class skills and world class markets. They want a Government responsive to their needs and to their concerns. They want a Parliament which reflects their thinking, not the internal bickering. They want the tax system reformed so that it is just and fair. They want peace unencumbered by Party politics. They want jobs and financial security for themselves and their children, and they want that fast. Above all, Mr. Speaker, they want hope for the future of this country and they want to have pride in this country. They are sick and tired of region pitted against region, of intolerant groups trying to impose views on other groups. They want what the Constitution promised them 116 years ago: peace, order and good Government.
In 1946 a great Canadian historian offered a very small and modest thought. It is so apt. He said:
In every generation Canadians have had to rework the miracle of their political existence. Canada has been created because there has existed within the hearts of its people, a determination to build for themselves an enduring home.
Mr. Speaker, the reason that the constituents of Rosedale, the people in Toronto with whom I talked, and I am sure all the constituents of all the Members of this House, want to have an election is that they want to get on with building that future, and this Government is in the road.

Mr. Speaker, I am always elevated by the speeches of the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie). I was disturbed by some of the comments he made with regard to the unemployment statistics. Is he confident that youth unemployment for educated youth who have gone through university and high school is 25 per cent? The latest figures 1 have seen indicate that the only group for which that figure is true is that of students who have not completed high school. For university graduates the unemployment rate is around 11 per cent. While it is unacceptable, for high school graduates the rate is around 18 per cent. The over-all average youth unemployment rate today is not 25 per cent but 18 per cent. This is still totally unacceptable but it is far less than the figure that the Hon. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too listened with interest to the comments made by the Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie). I thought they were thin. We will read his comments here with interest. He stood in the House and told us what people want. That is substantial and that is important. He did not tel! us anything about what he believes. He did not tell us anything about what he would do. While trying to pretend that he was offering something to people, he acutally failed the real test. He did not offer the people of this country his positive views and thereby give them an opportunity to judge which course of action they would like.
Mr. Speaker, that is the whole character of this motion and this debate. This is political fluff today. It is a waste of time. It is a rag-tag collection of tired cliches. We have seen this motion in the House over the over again. The Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the man who signed the motion, is a typical Tory. The motion and his speech today really represent his best contributions. He has a highly specialized skill, the skill of opposing. They offer no facts. They certainly offer no economic facts. If they were to take some of their statements out of the House and into the private sector they would not have a prayer of getting a job, because some of these statements do not hold water and do not earn anybody's respect. In the House those same statements are used to threaten courses of action and to threaten the basis for the livelihood and prosperity of some of our people.
The Mississauga News saw this very clearly and they treated the whole thing in a symbolic way recently. The Member for Yukon visited my riding. When he came, they ran his picture on November 2 and said the following things about him:
Conservative House Leader Erik Nielsen was the guest speaker last week at a fund-raising dinner for Mississauga North federal candidate Bob Horner. Nielsen was late for the dinner because of a filibuster in the House of Commons Friday.
They did not say anything about his speech because he did not say anything in his speech. They did not say anything about the crowd who were there. I am told the crowd was not
big enough to start a fight. That is so typical of the Conservative Party.
On the same weekend the Liberal Party in my riding held a dinner as well. We charged the 500 people $5 a couple, and we made money. The Tory Party charged $75 and served up a guy whose description in the newspaper is solely limited to that of a man who contributes to a filibuster in the House of Commons. That is all they have to say about him. That is all we can say about the Opposition in its offerings today. It is a filibuster. It is empty fluff. They are only for their capacity to oppose.
This same hollow motion and this same hollow speech have been repeated now for 20 years. For 20 years the Tory Party has been losing the very elections that it calls for in this motion. The same defeats follow the same hollow ideas.
I was quite amused the other day at a comment from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in answer to a recent question on the economy in the House of Commons. Statistics Canada had just reported some more good economic news and the Prime Minister stood up and said:
I was wondering this morning how the Opposition would manage to seek grief because unemployment had fallen for the seventh consecutive month and the figures are good and encouraging. I am interested in seeing that the Opposition can still put a sad face on good news.
That is exactly what we are seeing in this motion today. This imaginary tale of woe flies in the face of the reality in our country. It flies in the face of the fact that our economy is recovering. It flies in the face of enormous consumer confidence that is building and helping to regenerate that recovery. It flies in the face of serious attack against the unemployment tragedy in our country. It flies in the face of positive policies that are bringing back our positive economic strength.
