Policies like our short-term job creation program that are helping people facing severe disaster in their own lives. Policies brought out in the April budget that generated and rekindled business confidence. Policies like the special recovery projects that are speeding up Government investment and bringing it on line now when it is needed. Policies like our ongoing emphasis on trade and international relations. Those are the policies that this imaginary tale of woe flies in the face of.
My friend from Halifax called out that he would like an election. I would remind him of something that the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker said in Lethbridge way back in 1962. He said, "I would never have been Prime Minister if the Gallup polls had their way." Perhaps in the light of all their enthusiasm across the way sparked by the Gallup poll our good friends over there would like to keep Mr. Diefenbaker's reminders in mind. The Liberal Party is proud to stand up and
November 15, 1983

base an election campaign on the policies that we followed over the past five years.
Let us compare the programs that we have offered and the kind of hollow opposition that has been offered by the other side. Mr. Speaker, we believe that Canada is part of the whole world. We believe that, despite the desire by the Opposition to overlook that very simple obvious fact. That is why the six and five program was introduced. It kept us in line with our world competitors. It helped us to keep up our standards in world trade. It helped us to rebuild our export industries and to recover the lost jobs in the export industries. It helped us to keep in step with the recovery all over the world.
What was the Tory Party doing when that program was introduced? They voted against it and fought against it. They spoke against it. That was the end of their contribution to anything in that vein.
We in the Party believe that Canada is part of the world. That is why we have encouraged aggressive trade policies and that is why in this Parliament we expanded the Export Development Corporation. That is why in this Parliament we initiated Canagrex. What was the Tory answer to that? Their answer was a filibuster in the Elouse of Commons and in the committees from people like the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and the Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens). They could not stomach any longer the idea of supporting the Export Development Corporation, so they wanted to fight it despite the best interests of the country. They wanted to fight it to the point where the Business Council on National Issues sent a telegram, the day after another successful filibuster, pleading with the committee to get on with it because the Corporation was needed by businesses and exporters all across this country. That was the Tories' answer and that was the public's answer to their activities.
We believe that Canada is indeed part of the world. That is why we proposed a revitalized rail system. That is why we have just finished an intense debate, following two years of consultation coast to coast with Canadians on the Crow rate. Through these kinds of revitalization in our rail industry, we create the confidence that we can deliver our products to the outside world. Our customers come to believe that they can rely on us. Our customers believe that our suppliers are reliable sources of these vital products for them.
We have supported the change in the Crow rate because in this case there is a clear link between better trade, better railroads and better jobs for all Canadians. But what happened? The Tory Party voted against the Crow rate. They voted against new industry for western Canada.

speechtext:
There is not a whimper from them now when that kind of fact is brought out. When they want an election, we will be happy to bring those gentle facts from the record to the attention of a few Canadians.
Not only do we live in an open world, we believe that we must foster and nourish Canadian industry within that context. That is why we have FIRA-to set standards and to screen applicants who want to come to Canada. It is not to keep them away or to discourage them but simply to let them know that when they invest in this country they must follow Canadian standards for the benefit of the Canadian economy and Canadian society.
That is why we have the national energy plan, so that our wealth and resources can be developed for our own use and prosperity. What do we see from the Tory Party? They want to tear down FIRA and destroy the National Energy Program. We see a leader in the Party who cannot wait to pander to every foreign carpetbagger with any kind of business idea. We see a finance critic who ran his leadership campaign recently on the entire thesis of open trade and complete vulnerability to the United States. We see the foreign critic of that Party for whom Washington's every wish is his deepest command.
We on this side of the House believe in a co-operative effort between the Government and the people to build our country. That is why we are proud to support Petro-Canada. That is why we do not want to abandon the Canadair efforts. That is why we are proud of our Crown corporations. That is why we are ready to join with business and give them incentives to become involved in vital activities.
When we examine the Tory record, we see memories of the Avro-Arrow and we hear hollow squawks about European socialism as the thin disguises for their destructive programs.
Finally, we on this side of the House believe that Canadians should have a decent safety net for the days when they personally get into trouble or when our economy gets into trouble. When one examines our record over the past year, one can see a proud record of help for Canadians in the depth of really tough economic times-. We put $4.5 billion into the special recovery program. We have the National Training Act to help people whose skills are outdated or businesses which need to upgrade the skills of valuable employees. We have seen the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) put an emphasis on a decent medicare system, despite the activities of Tories in the provincial Governments from coast to coast. We have job sharing under the Unemployment Insurance Program. As well, we have the NEED Program, Canada Works and Summer Works, all of which are short term

job-creation programs intended to bridge tough times and help people have a job for a few days or weeks until their old jobs return.
But what we see in this very motion is the revealing of the real Tory attitude. Their attitude is that we should give the rich a nice tax break despite the homilies from the Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie). I would say to him again that 1 doubt the people in Regent Park are really worried about having some kind of special rollover provisions on our RRSPs, or other cute little tax breaks. What they want are jobs. They want a fair tax system that taxes people from coast to coast equally. We see Members on the other side propose ideas to help the rich keep their money and hide it from the taxman at the expense of the poor who must carry those burdens. No one engaged in such vitriolic debate as some of those Members when the MacEachen budget was introduced. The very heart of their complaints was that the rich would have to pay more and pay their share. That was very clear in all of their debates.
We offered a chance for a fair and more even tax system. In this motion we find that that is supposed to create a lack of confidence in the Government. What else do we see in this motion? We see a direct attack on the funding for the safety net. We see a direct attack on the use of Government resources to help people in trouble. This comes out very clearly when the two Members from St. John's rise. The Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) wrings his hands, full of pity, and the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) says that we must cut the deficit. Who is it that has the greater power and greater influence? It is the deficit cutter, the one who wants to take a direct run at the safety and prosperity of ordinary working Canadians.
This motion is thin. The speeches we have heard, particularly the one from the Member for Yukon, are outstandingly thin. After this debate, when all of these cliches are dragged out and these tired criticisms are dragged out, we should always remember the little warning we had from Gerard Pelletier back in 1971 who told us that "Alarmism is the real temptation of opposition". That is what we are hearing in all of this. It is a faint hope that they will stir up fires and drag out discontented people without being caught in any of the real choices or real options of Government.
Let us just go down the list that I have given in my comments. Let us note that we on the Liberal side believe that Canada must take part in the entire world and not hide. Here on this side we believe that we must help our own economy to grow. What do the Tories do? They fight against FIR A. They vote against the National Energy Program and they try to open our doors to any kind of carpetbagger that comes along. We believe on the Liberal side that Canada must use co-operative efforts between the people and their Government. What we see is two clear-cut cases of deliberate and malicious attacks on Petro-Canada and on Canadair. On this side of the House we believe that Canada must create safety nets for ordinary Canadians. What do we
see on the other side? Plaintive pleas on behalf of the rich, and deliberate attacks against the spending that funds and supports safety nets for the poor.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the earliest days no principle has been more central to our system of justice than that the law must be understood and that it must be applied fairly and even-handedly. When ordinary citizens are incapable of understanding how the law applies to them or when laws are enforced unevenly, democracy perishes and despotism is born.
In Canada we take pride in the fairness of a system of laws designed to protect the citizen when his rights conflict with the convenience of the state. One of the reasons Parliament acted two years ago to entrench the Charter of Rights in our Constitution was precisely to defend that principle. Yet, principles can become undermined to the point that they cease to have any relevance at all. By its sheer weight, big government can smother the rights of its citizens and overwhelm their ability even to insist upon fairness in their dealings with the state.
For Canadians in 1983, that is precisely what is happening in their relationship with the federal tax bureaucracy. We have a crazy-quilt Act that probably no one in Canada, either inside the Government or outside it, can claim to understand. Certainly 1 would be surprised if there were anyone in the House who is responsible for passing laws, including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres), who would claim to understand fully the Income Tax Act.
If those of us who write the law and those who enforce it are not fully knowledgeable about what it means, think of the position of ordinary Canadians-working persons, farmers or fishermen, artists, owners of small businesses and pensioners. How are they to negotiate the income tax morass without becoming lost in it? Indeed it is hard to see what they are to do when faced with laws they do not understand and with officials who have little interest in their plight.
A tax system like ours, based on voluntary reporting and payment, can only work as long as those affected by it feel they are being treated fairly. When respect for the law breaks down, or when people begin to feel they have become victims and no longer beneficiaries of the Government and its policies, growing numbers of citizens are prepared to break the law or to make enforcement as difficult as possible.
Increasingly that is what is happening in Canada today. The vast majority of Canadians are conscientious and law-abiding. They love their country and they are prepared to carry their fair share of its economic burden. However, when they begin to feel that their Government views them as criminals waiting to be caught, their respect for the law and their willingness to comply with it rapidly decline.
Here is how one chartered accountant from Toronto described the problem in a recent letter to me. He wrote:
I can see how upset my clients are with the unreasonable treatment that they are receiving. My advice is to file the documents and appeal when the notice of reassessment comes through. The obvious result is that the auditors are wasting their time because they don't accept the document and we don't accept the reassessment. My clients have to pay me for what they can see is unreasonable treatment and the tax department has to pay their employees for the wasted effort.
But 1 think that there is a larger impact in this. As someone recently said; the tax department is unfair and arbitrary so why should I be honest in reporting information on my tax return? I think that this attitude is much more common now than it was when I first started in the business. I advise my clients to file their returns correctly, but if taxpayers believe that they are being treated unfairly, they are much less inclined to be honest.
Members of Parliament on all sides of the House could quote from similar letters or refer to similar representations which have been made to them by chartered accountants, lawyers or other experts in the tax field. We have found two things happening frequently. First, the income tax laws become so complex that ordinary people feel trapped in the maze. Second, actions by the Department of National Revenue have often been so capricious and unfair as to estrange ordinary Canadians and make them feel that they are victims of their Government or that their Government is out to get them rather than simply requiring that they pay their fair share.
I cite this example, not because it is extraordinary but because it is typical of a growing number of complaints being received by every Member of Parliament. If the Government needs other authorities to convince it that the situation is serious and that it is rapidly growing worse, I could refer it to a book which was first published by a tax lawyer from Montreal. It is entitled, "How to Survive Canada's Tax Chaos". On the front cover of the book there is a quotation from a review in The Gazette of Montreal which read, "should be required for every Member of Parliament". Certainly I agree. It would be helpful if Members of Parliament on all sides of the House would read this book. They would gain some impression of the author's views of how the tax system has worked in Canada and how improvements could be made to make it more fair and equitable, to ensure that it functions in a better way and more successfully and to ensure that relations between the Government and the citizens of Canada are conducted in a more civilized fashion. Here is part of what the author wrote in his introduction:
Since the introduction of "tax reform" with all its complexities and inequities, I have noted a distinct deterioration in the "tax morality" of many taxpayers who hithertofore have been scrupulous in their accountability to the public treasury. Why? There are at least five discernible reasons for this development-
He then proceeded to list the five reasons he feels Canadians are losing faith in the tax system. The first reason listed was that many people have lost confidence in the Government's
November 15, 1983

ability to provide them and their families with any long-term security. That was in 1976. Surely since that time, as the Government has dragged Canada into a recession, that confidence has fallen even further.
The second reason which is advanced by the author is uncontrolled Government spending and bureaucracy. He elaborates on the point in this way:
Many taxpayers find no way to counter what they consider profligate government spending otherwise than through tax avoidance and often tax evasion. The growing list of government "white elephants" that have consumed billions of taxpayers' dollars, the failure of government to establish and abide by accepted financial controls as illustrated by the recent revelations of the Auditor General, the unacceptable level of remunerations, perquisites and retirement benefits enjoyed by certain of our "civil servants" which are virtually unmatched in the private sector, and the seeming disregard for the peoples' priorities, have all contributed to an attitude of hostility towards governments at all levels. Many maintain that hard-earned income is being expropriated by government in the guise of public necessity only to be in turn dispensed on ill-conceived public projects, to idle bureaucrats, and to indolent welfare beneficiaries both individual or corporate and that this waste of tax dollars is justification for resistance to growing government fiscal demands. This resistance may take many forms but tax evasion is certainly one of them.
The third cause listed by this author is tax inequities. The author states that:
-there is no doubt in my mind that the failure of our tax system to achieve "tax neutrality" (i.e. that taxpayers in the same circumstances should bear the same tax burden) is also contributing to the practice of tax evasion.
Two other reasons listfcd by the author are that a small proportion of the population will always want to evade taxes and that the tax system is too complex. On the latter point, he concludes:
I believe that the establishment of requirements clearly destined to be ignored or disobeyed has the effect of undermining the entire system.
Who was that tax lawyer from Montreal who wrote the book "How to Survive Canada's Tax Chaos", Mr. Speaker? He was the Prime Minister's tax laywer, a man named Donald J. Johnston. He is currently the Minister of State for Economic Development in the Cabinet of this Government.
A review from the Montreal Gazette appeared on the front of that book as saying that the book should be required reading for every Member of Parliament. I would suggest that that is entirely correct. The first place to start would be on the Treasury benches themselves because when the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) was simply a tax lawyer and was representing Canadians at that level, he had a very good grasp of some of the problems which are confronted by Canadians when dealing with the Government. He had a prescription for ways to correct those problems. Yet today, Mr. Speaker, we find that he has been swallowed up in this massive bureaucracy against which he previously railed and we find that he is part of a Cabinet which is indifferent to the plight of ordinary Canadians and which is not concerned about reforming the system, making it more equitable and ensuring that the confidence of the people in Government is increased. That is why 1 agree very much with what was quoted on the front of that book. This book should indeed be required reading for every Member of Parliament.
Supply
The statements which 1 quoted were written in 1976. Today we have a tax system that is far more complex, far less equitable and far more subject to bureaucratic caprice than it was seven years ago.
In September of this year, Hon. Members will recall that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce met with the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance to recommend ways to improve our tax legislation and its administration. In its brief, the Chamber complained of inordinate delays arising from bureaucratic inefficiencies. It also reported this finding:
There is a growing perception across the country that Revenue Canada is becoming more and more aggressive in its attitude towards the assessing and collection of income taxes. No one disputes the right of Revenue Canada to collect the full amount of tax to which it is entitled, but there appears to be a significant growth in the number of frivolous or poorly based assessments, often issued without the benefit of discussion with the taxpayer. In addition, the collection officers then insist on payment of the tax owing, even though it might be obvious on a cursory review that the assessment will be reversed on appeal.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a blunt and candid assessment of the Department's procedures. However, the Chamber of Commerce is not alone in its concerns. On May 28, The Globe and Mail reported that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association had struck an ad hoc committee to consider the assessing procedures of the National Revenue Department. The article quoted a number of authorities who were concerned about the Department's aggressive tactics. If the Government were serious about its relationship with Canadians, it could implement reforms today to begin to correct this situation.
There is no element of this problem that is more serious than the inequity that occurs when moving from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. One finds that the law is applied unevenly as one moves from place to place. A recent example of this was brought to the attention of the House, and that was the tax treatment of members of symphony orchestras. The tax department's interpretation in the case of the Montreal Symphony Orchestra was entirely different from the way in which it interpreted the position of members of the Toronto Symphony Orchestra. That is not atypical. It is something which happens all too often in the system and something that must be addressed.
1 would like to refer the House to an article that appeared in The Toronto Sunday Star of November 6, 1983. The author of that article, Mr. George Brett, was referring to comments made by a lawyer named Paul Schnier. In that article, the author says this:
Schnier adds that some district tax offices are tougher than others to deal with (though the taxpayer must deal with his own office and so has no choice).
"Hamilton is notorious and Kitchener is another tough one," he says. "Toronto, because it deals with more (tax) professionals, is in a position where it has to be a little more accommodating.
"The auditor in Toronto knows he's dealing not only with the taxpayer but his accountant or lawyer as well-and tax practitioners aren't easy to push around."
This tax lawyer says that one's treatment at the hands of the Government under the Income Tax Act depends to a great extent upon where in the country one lives and which office one must deal with. Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is something that is unfair and that attacks the confidence of the people in the administration of the income tax system.

November 15, 1983
Supply
There are a number of things which can be done to correct the problems that we have referred to today. First, it is time for a review of ways to make our tax laws more intelligible. When growing numbers of people find that they cannot fill out their own tax returns without someone else's help and when the cost of assistance in filling out one's return is not even deductible for individual taxpayers, the system has broken down badly. The Leader of my Party has struck a task force that will report in a matter of months on ways in which a Progressive Conservative Government would simplify the tax system.
Second, it is time to remove some of the clear inequities from the system. When the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) was Minister of Finance, he attempted to give Canada's hard-pressed family farmers a break when he proposed capital gains tax relief for family farms.
Third, it is time to take a fresh look at some of the special advantages which the law gives to the tax department. As an article in the October 23 edition of the Toronto Star recently pointed out, the onus of proof is on Revenue Canada only in a small number of instances; for example, when it is prosecuting, when it reassesses a tax return more than four years old and when it is levying penalties. In most other cases, the onus of proof is on the taxpayer to explain any discrepancies. Additionally, it is hard to justify allowing the tax department to force payments while the assessment is being disputed.
Fourth, and perhaps most important of all, the Minister of National Revenue has a responsibility to ensure that his officials treat taxpayers with courtesy and respect. Every Canadian would expect tax cheaters to face prosecution, but for the vast majority of people whose greatest offence was to make an honest error, there is no justification whatsoever for anything but polite and helpful treatment by the Government. That tone should be set by the Minister himself and clear instructions should go from him to each of his employees indicating that strong-arm tactics will not be tolerated.
There has probably never been a time either in this or in any other country where a call from the tax department has been particularly welcome. I doubt that any of us will ever see that day in the future. However, relations between taxpayers and the Government have now reached the lowest point in our history and the breakdown in our tax system can only worsen unless the Government acts now.
There is no need for the atmosphere of mutual distrust which exists today between the federal Government and the Canadian people. It is perhaps too late for the present administration to reverse that sad condition, but it is not too late for a new Government with fresh ideas, with a desire to serve and not to rule and with faith in our citizens to begin the task. Rebuilding the confidence of Canadians in their Government is a challenge worthy of a new team and it is urgent that the work begin now.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Schroder (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62(9)-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-GOVERNMENT LEGISLATIVE ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have the opportunity to speak in this debate. There are two
issues contained in the motion which concern me, and one is the idea that we have used closure or time allocation on many occasions. The second is the idea that what the people of Canada want now is an election. I was interested to hear many speakers, including the last speaker, say that Members of the Party on the other side have some fresh ideas. They must still be germinating because I have not heard many of them.
I would like to warn the people of Canada that in light of the fact that there are no ideas and we do not know what the policies of the Opposition would be if they were in Government, they should think of what Napoleon said when inspecting his troops toward the end of the battle of Waterloo. Following his inspection of that rather rag-tag group of desolate beings, he was asked by someone what he thought their effect would be on the enemy. Napoleon was reputed to have said, "I don't know about the enemy, but they sure scare the hell out of me". When we think about the Opposition, that is the sort of feeling I get. I am a little frightened.
With respect to time allocation or closure motions that we have had, I find the attitude taken by the Opposition in bringing forth this motion today to be quite strange, to say the least. They wish this House to condemn the use of, not closure but time allocation on various Bills passed during the session. On the face of it, they do not wish to take account of the merit of these Bills, the time that was consumed in debating the Bills, or the surrounding circumstances, including the impact that failure to pass the legislation might have had.
Good management in all things, particularly good management of time, has always been a virtue, yet these are exactly the issues which must be addressed by the Government in taking action to limit debate. In fact, before time allocation takes place, there is a time period set aside during which Members on both sides of the House may debate the motion for time allocation.
Let us take two of the Bills that have been singled out by Members opposite, Bill C-131 and Bill C-132 to amend the Old Age Security Act and the Family Allowance Act. Both of these pieces of legislation were intended to give effect to portions of the six and five program announced in the budget of June 18, 1983. The program was designed to tackle the very serious problem of inflation by setting identified goals for cost increases in both the public and private sectors and then by taking the lead in a broad range of ideas within the federal authority. It was an effort to end the inflationary psychology that had taken hold of this country and was keeping inflation at high rates of around 12 per cent. As part of this effort, the Government felt it necessary for a period of two years to set limits on the indexation of family allowance and basic old age security pension. In so doing, it was the Government's stated intention to enlist the participation of Canadian families and Canadian senior citizens in this effort to show how important and serious the six and five program really was. Clearly this was a difficult step to take and special protective measures had to be instituted at the same time to safeguard those with low
November 15, 1983

incomes, as 1 will discuss later. In both cases, the Bills were introduced in the House in October, 1982, to take effect from January 1, 1983.
In the case of Bill C-131 to amend the Old Age Security Act, the amending legislation was introduced for second reading on November 18, 1982, and was debated by 28 Members, including 23 Opposition Members, seven Progressive Conservatives and six New Democrats, up to the point of time allocation.
The terms and effects of the legislation had by that time been very thoroughly debated indeed, well beyond the point where any additional insights or views were being added. It came to the point where the Government had to consider the effects on the parliamentary process, on the six and five program and on the public if passage were to be further delayed.
These effects were serious. First, time was being lost for the debate of other important legislation. Second, the whole psychological effort, the seriousness of the Government's determination to ensure that inflation would be brought down, was being laid open to question, and this could have led to a return to the inflationary viewpoint if matters had gone on indefinitely. Last and most important, uncertainty that was being created in the minds of the pensioners had to be of concern. They did not know what to expect. Would their January pension cheque be limited or would it not? What was the amount going to be? They needed to know this so that they could plan accordingly.
The provisions of Bill C-131 had been designed with great care. The old age security pension is indexed four times a year rather than once a year so that its real value stays as constant as possible. However, the 6 per cent and 5 per cent limits were annual targets. To meet these goals within the OAS program, the indexation of the basic pension was to be limited to no more than 1.5 per cent over the December 1982 rate in the first quarter of 1983, no more than 3 per cent in the second quarter, 4.5 per cent in the third quarter and 6 per cent in the fourth quarter.
As it turned out, the fully indexed basic pension in the first quarter of 1983 was $251.12, while the limiting amount under the Bill was $250.62, a difference of 50 cents. It was for that amount, 50 cents a month, that Opposition Members were acting to create uncertainty and anxiety in the minds of pensioners by delaying passage of the Bill.
Furthermore, it was not all pensioners who were subject to a limit on their indexation. All low income pensioners, in fact all pensioners who received any portion of the Guaranteed Income Supplement, were guaranteed by the legislation not to lose a single cent. The legislation provided that recipients of the supplement, who make up more than half the pension population, would have their supplement fully indexed and then increased further to offset the effect of the six and five limits on their basic OAS pension. These pensioners then were assured that they would be no worse off after the legislation was passed, but the delay in passage was no doubt causing them some worry.
Supply
Despite these factors, it was clear that Members of the Opposition were not prepared to agree to a reasonable length of time for debate prior to passage of the legislation. Instead, there were clear statements made that the New Democrats at least would continue to present speakers as long as the bill was in debate in order to delay its passage to the longest extent possible. This is the climate in which the Government decided that it must move for time allocation.
Even so, time allocation only limited further debate on second reading of the Bill, which was then sent to committee on December 10, 1982. In committee, the Bill received a further and extremely thorough examination in four days of hearings before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs before it was reported back to the House without amendment on December 21, 1982.
It was then debated at the report stage until January 31, 1983, when time allocation had to be moved a second time to finish off report and third stages. At that point, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) noted that some 71 Members had spoken at various stages of the passage of the Bill. After a further time allocation debate, another full day at report stage and a final day of debate on third reading, the Bill went to the Senate on February, 1983.
Very similar circumstances were faced by Bill C-132, a legislation to limit the indexation of family allowances for two years. That Bill did not require time allocation to obtain second reading. In fact, it was moved to committee after two days of vigorous debate in the House and was reported back after three days of hearings by the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. However, at report stage, it again became clear that debate was being extended for the sole purpose of delaying passage, and time allocation had to be sought. At that point, 32 Members had already participated in debate on the Bill at its various stages.
As with Bill C-131, the concerns of the Government extended to more than simply the time of the House which was being used up in debate for the sake of delay, while other important legislation was awaiting passage. There was also concern about the uncertainty and worry which were being created for recipients, although by this time the limitation had been applied in January, 1983 to restrict family allowance increases to 6 per cent. More important for these recipients, however, was the delay created by opposition to another piece of six and five legislation, namely, Bill C-139.
As in the case of Bill C-131, the Government had been careful to ensure that low-income families could be protected against the effects of limiting their family allowance increases. In the case of old age security, the protection came through the income-tested Guaranteed Income Supplement. In the case of family allowances, however, the appropriate vehicle for protection was the refundable child tax credit which is provided for low-income and middle-income families under the Income Tax Act. To offset the effect of the limit on family allowances, the Minister of Finance announced a special one-

November 15, 1983
Supply
time $50 increase in the child tax credit for 1982, raising it from $293 to $343 per child. This increase was intended to balance in advance the expected reduction in family allowance over the two-year restraint period for these low-income and middle-income families. However, the increased child tax credit could not be refunded until Bill C-139, the legislation amending the Income Tax Act, was passed. This again took a great deal of time while the Bill was being debated in the House. That delay in passing C-139 held up the child tax credit payments for many mothers.
If 1 may say so, Mr. Speaker, the experience of Canadian mothers having their child tax credits delayed, provides a very good example of the type of circumstances which support the responsible application of time allocation. We heard this morning some talk about the fact that Parliament has lost relevance in the eyes of many of the people and they were saying, "Why do you not get on with the job?" Time allocation in this case did help in allowing us to get on with the job.
Let me now turn to perhaps the most important point in discussing the wisdom of this motion as it refers to Bills C-131 and C-132, and that is the merits of the legislation itself. During the course of the debate, which some Members of the Opposition clearly feel was not long enough, there was certainly plenty of time for Opposition Members to say many incorrect things about the six and five program and about the purpose and the effects of Bills C-131 and C-132. There was time for them to suggest that the Bills were deindexing family allowances and pensions, when they were continuing indexation, albeit subject to limits. There was time for them to suggest that the legislation was simply an effort to save money, when in fact the savings were less in the first year than the cost of the child tax credit increase, and every effort was being made to minimize the effect of the limits by bringing inflation down. There was time for Opposition Members to quote and repeat figures showing that pensioners would lose hundreds of dollars, even after actual figures for the first quarter were released showing a difference of only 50 cents a month once the Bill took effect, and only for pensioners with incomes too high to qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
To put it mildly, it is obvious that many Hon. Members of the Opposition portrayed the legislation as something which was dangerous, misguided and would create hardship among vulnerable segments of our society. So it is certainly a welcome opportunity to look back now at the end of 1983 and be able to confirm that these Bills did serve the purpose they were intended to serve, without harming Canadian families or senior citizens.
These very favourable conclusions stem largely from the results of the six and five program. All Hon. Members know what has happened to the inflation rate in Canada. It has gone from an unacceptable high rate in 1982 to its lowest level in years in 1983. The 12-month rate to September, 1983 stood at 5 per cent. For old age security pensioners, this has meant that the limits set by Bill C-131 have not had to be applied in the last three quarters. The amount of the old age security benefits right now is exactly the same as it would have been in the
absence of the legislation. This is due to the measures taken by the Government. The OAS basic pension is the same as it would have been in the absence of the legislation, as I said. I feel that bears repeating.
The full indexation of old age security to the end of 1983 has been held within the limits allowed, so that the amount of benefit for the last three quarters has not been at all affected by the legislation. Some pensioners did lose a total of one dollar as a result of the limit applied to their February and March OAS cheques, but that is all, up to this point.
For family allowances recipients, the drop in the inflation rate has meant that the over-all impact on the value of their allowances is less than originally expected. Given that inflation is now running at 5 per cent, the limited indexation increase of 5 per cent in family allowances this coming January will be doing a good job of maintaining the real value of the benefit. Furthermore, since Bill C-132 was passed, the Minister of Finance announced in his April, 1983 budget that the special $50 per child increase in the 1982 child tax credit will not be removed. Instead, the credit will remain at the $343 per child level for 1983, and this amount will be fully indexed for 1984 and subsequent years. This means that neither old age security pensioners nor family allowance recipients have been hurt by Bills C-131 and C-132 in the way in which some Opposition Members suggested they would. In fact, we might ask ourselves who has benefited most from the drop in inflation which has taken place since the six and five program was introduced.
One group which has deservedly benefited from lower inflations is pensioners with fixed annuities and unindexed private pensions. These pensioners were unable to protect the value of their pensions which were being eaten away by double-digit inflation. Even 5 per cent is too much inflation if you have a fixed income, but it is definitely preferable to 12 per cent. Another group which may have benefited is young families in the low and middle income ranges. These were the people who were hardest hit by inflationary mortgage rates and by general costs which for many rose faster than their wages.
This then was the record of this legislation. It did no harm to those who most need the social benefits. At the same time, it was an important contribution to the objective of the Government; to help bring inflation under control by reducing the inflationary expectations in the country. Clearly, the six and five program worked to the point at which it has surpassed our expectations.
Time allocation is a tool of the parliamentary process which must not be utilized lightly. Its use must be justified by the circumstances and defended by Governments in debate. Nevertheless, it is a legitimate instrument to which responsible Government must resort for good and sufficient reasons, as in the case of Bills C-131 and C-132. Accordingly, I must advise you that I cannot agree with the motion which has been laid before the House today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am not in British Columbia and thank goodness that matter is hopefully over. But I wanted to point that out to show the hypocritical and selective nature of the motion and the position taken by the Official Opposition.
In the debate today the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), and a number of speakers from the Conservative Party, talked about energy and petroleum taxes. 1 took the opportunity of getting a copy of the infamous speech by the Leader of the Official Opposition at a fund raising dinner in the Calgary Convention Centre on November 8, 1983. He talked about some problems in the National Energy Program with which I have some passing familiarity. The motion mentions energy taxes, and the Leader of the Opposition said this:
One, the cash flow of the companies involved was gravely impaired by the federal "tax grab"-
When the Official Opposition presents a motion like this, and when its Leader makes a speech like this, it really has to get over some very serious naivete in dealing with energy in this country. The oil companies of this country always want more "cash flow". They did ten years ago, they do today and they will tomorrow. They always want more money. The poor Leader of the Opposition is getting sucked in to giving more money to these companies. How do you finance a Government, Mr. Speaker? You have to get taxes and you have to choose whom you are going to tax. Are you going to tax consumers, the poor, the middle-income earners, the pensioners? Or are you going to tax the oil companies and banks, some of the people who can afford to pay? Here we have the first indication of the kind of policy presented by the Opposition. Finally we are hitting a moving target here. They are about to change the tax structure to help the oil companies, and it will result in penalizing indirectly the average ordinary Canadian. The second thing the Leader of the Official Opposition said in that speech was this:
Two, there was so much obvious retroactivity and confiscation in the NEP that investors lost whatever trust and confidence they had in the federal Government.
That is the United States line, Mr. Speaker. That is exactly what Ambassador Paul Robinson said. This is a branch plant economic position. When you take this kind of position on economic policy-that is, we will follow what the Americans want and open wide to American investment-and then take the same position on foreign policy, a "me too" Reaganism, then you have a complete change, and this is why the motion surprises me. You have a complete historic change in the modern Conservative Party. This is now a continentalist Party. It is for big oil, and make no mistake about it.

November 15, 1983
Supply
Have you seen the ads that the Canadian Petroleum Association has every night on TV, Mr. Speaker? I urge Canadians to watch these ads. If they flip channels they will probably see them. They talk about how they are going to help Canada and co-operate with the federal Government and take a fair return and so on. The Canadian Petroleum Association is big American oil. That is who controls the CPA. That is who is giving this line about more cash flow, about retroactivity and confiscation under the NEP. My goodness, Mr. Speaker, there are lots of things to attack in the NEP: the pricing scheme, the give-away PIP grants, where we are doing exploration and so on. But they are taking the American line. We are still an independent country. The Americans are our allies, but we are an independent country and we have to remember that. Is this what the modern Conservative Party has come to? John A. Macdonald would not be turning in his grave, he would be spinning in his grave if he could read this Calgary speech of the Leader of the Opposition.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say something else about this motion today. It seems to me that the Conservatives have missed the mark on the non-confidence aspect of the Government. It should not be in energy. It should not be in Canagrex or the Crow and so on. It should be in the handling of the economy. If we had had a chance to put forward a motion, we would have tackled head on today the most important thing that has happened around here in a little while. That was the conference on high tech last week. My Party and I have no confidence in the way that the Government is handling the revolution in high technology and the way that the conference happened last week. The Government spent $500,000 on a conference on high tech that was virtually Government propaganda and that missed the whole social implication of high technology. The highlight of the conference apparently was Senator Lawson's offcolour speech telling dirty jokes. That shows you the shallowness of the conference. Basically, labour was not at the conference. The largest labour group, the CLC, the legitimate group, was not represented at that conference. The reason that they were not there is that they never thought that the Government would look at the underlying problems of high tech. There was an underlying assumption from the conference that we do not have to deal with labour in the future because high tech will replace the labour unions and they will be gone. There was that very important and very serious assumption. There was also an assumption that high tech was a good thing. There was no talk about the deskilling effect of high technology or how it affects working people.
I think that what the Government was most incompetent in was in the handling of that conference and in its handling of the high technology revolution. The fact is that people are being affected by high tech and the Canadian worker should have a say in how high tech is developed. They are not modern Luddites, the people who knocked machines when they came in at the beginning of the industrial revolution. The Canadian worker has a legitimate concern. I say this to the Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) who was at the conference.
Look at British Columbia. When the worker is up against the wall, when you take away job security and seniority and you make things so insecure for the worker, the worker will fight back. One thing we learned in British Columbia last month is that the teachers will fight back. No one expected the teachers to go out the way they did. No one expected some of those other unions to join. There is a lesson to be learned, and the Government should learn it. The lesson is that the Canadian worker is not going to sit back and lose his or her job needlessly. There is a great feeling of insecurity out there, and the Government should address this in the upcoming high technological revolution. In offices secretaries are worried about losing their jobs. Women especially will be affected by this change. It is coming faster and faster all the time. We have to deal with it.
I would like to say one other thing about the high technological revolution. The Government should get on with the job of appointing an all-parliamentary committee or some committee that really has labour on it. I mean the CLC people who have really gone into some of the problems associated with high technology. The Government should listen to people like Heather Menzies when she speaks articulately about how technological change will affect women and how the deskilling affects the job. In fact, what we are going to have is a few high technocrats making lots of money and the rest of us being technopeasants of this new era. We will lose the middle class in Canada. That is a fundamental change in the Canadian economy and society.
I hope it is through negligence rather than bad will, but the Government is missing the boat here. It should get this out in public and have a public commission or a committee of this House of Commons and it should bring in all the labour groups. It should not have Senator Lawson come in and tell a few dirty jokes, but it should go to some other teamster people in the country. In Vancouver they can speak articulately about labour matters. The Government should speak to the CLC people.
I would like to conclude by moving a motion. I move:
That the present motion be amended by inserting the following after the word "borrowing":
"and for accepting the advice of the Official Opposition when they urged the Government to abandon the Crow rate and increase the public debt through additional borrowing to grant billions of dollars to private sector oil companies."
I am told that the motion has been approved by the Chair. I propose to move that motion, and I do so. I believe you have a copy of the motion, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to conclude by saying that in the NDP we think that we have made our position very clear as an Opposition Party. We opposed the Crow rate from the beginning. We consistently opposed it. Today in the House of Commons my colleague from Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) asked a question of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy). He said that one day after the Crow passed the railways were laying off people in Winnipeg at the rail yards. The Government promised that great things would happen after the change in the Crow rate. Right away we see lay-offs. We were skeptical
November 15, 1983

and we were right. I think we are going to see that the change in the Crow rate is not all that was promised and it is really going to hurt the farmer in the prairie Provinces.
Mr. Speaker, this amendment covers the notion that was brought up time and time again in debate today, that is, the energy policy, of borrowing and of giving billions of dollars in petroleum grants to the poor private oil companies which moan and groan and whose moans and groans have been accepted by the Leader of the Conservative Party. 1 do not know what he is going to do if he ever gets to be Prime Minister, because he is going to have to choose between Premier Davis, who is going to want low energy prices, and Premier Lougheed, who is going to want high energy prices. As the Leader of the Opposition said in his speech, they are going to solve all the problems because, "It is time for energy policy in this country to be established around the table of consensus. It is time for co-operative efforts. It is time for this country to begin realizing the tremendous potential we all know it has." That is fluff. That is shallowness. A real Prime Minister, a real leader, has to deal with and solve conflicting regional viewpoints. These regional viewpoints killed the former Conservative Leader, the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), who could not survive the problems between Premier Davis and Premier Lougheed. Let us not have this fluff from the Official Opposition. Let us not have these inconsistencies, as the Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) said. Let us have some real policy. Let Canadians know what you are going to do.

When its Leader was speaking in the 1980 election, in some previous reincarnation, after 12 years he suddenly found that our oil industry was controlled by multinational oil companies that were basically American.
